# Kai Gao

I am a 6th year PhD student in economics at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, specializing in industrial organization and environmental economics. My research studies how regulation changes consumer behavior and firms' product design.

I am on the academic job market in 2026–27.

## Working Papers {#working-papers}

::: {.paper}
### Beyond the Label: Do Ecodesign Regulations Reduce Real-World Energy Use? (Job Market Paper) {#beyond-the-label-do-ecodesign-regulations-reduce-real-world-energy-use-jmp}

[Paper (PDF)](files/Gao_JMP.pdf)

I study the 2021 European washing-machine energy-label reform. Firms improve Eco efficiency while energy use rises in other wash programs. An equilibrium model of product design, purchases, and program choice quantifies the implications for actual electricity use and welfare.

<details>
<summary>Abstract</summary>

This paper studies how ecodesign regulation shapes product design and consumer welfare when compliance is tied to a single operating mode rather than overall real-world use. I examine the German washing machine market following the 2021 EU reform, which rescaled energy-efficiency labels and imposed a duration constraint on the regulated Eco program. Combining product-program-level data with a new laundry-habit survey, I document substantial scope for regulatory leakage, as the regulated Eco program accounts for only about 10 percent of reported wash cycles. Following the reform, Eco energy consumption declines, while energy consumption increases in hotter Cotton programs. To explain these patterns, I develop and estimate an equilibrium model of endogenous product entry, pricing, and program design that incorporates household wash-program choice. The estimates show that firms respond to regulatory incentives by improving measured Eco efficiency while offering more energy-intensive Cotton programs to attract households that prefer longer wash cycles. Counterfactuals imply that the Eco-duration cap raises reference-inclusive electricity consumption by 11.4 percent relative to retaining energy labels without the cap. Broadening the efficiency index to include Cotton 60°C reduces gross electricity consumption by 6.0 percent and increases consumer surplus relative to an uncapped Eco-only index.

</details>

:::

::: {.paper}
### What Drives the Repowering of Wind Turbines? Evidence from the Danish Wind Energy Industry

I study how renewable-energy subsidies affect the replacement of aging wind turbines in Denmark. A dynamic model of investment and replacement examines how support for existing installations shapes the timing of technology upgrades and evaluates alternative subsidy designs.
:::
